warmup.text: Last lesson, Isaac saw something nobody else could see. Today you find out what it meant. Start with the warm-up. The DOL sentence comes straight from Chapter 4, and it moves. Then read the poem and listen for who is talking in it.

words.text: Today you match each word to its root, and you read this week's words in sentences from the book. In the river game, say each word slowly and listen for where your voice stops.

reading.text: Read Chapters 3 and 4 in your book. These are hard chapters. Isaac sees more visions, and then something happens that is not a vision at all. Take your time. When you finish, try the quick check, then the Read Like a Writer box.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapters 3 and 4, and then a draft of your own moment. Pick one moment from your list. Write it from the inside, with I, the way Isaac does.

do: Read today's skill.
Tap the lens you will use today.
Notice one detail Isaac warns you about.
how.why: Isaac tells the story as someone who already knows the ending. Noticing his warnings shows you how his voice works.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Fix the second sentence out loud.
Tap Check My Work to compare.
how.why: Strong verbs and a subject that acts make a sentence easy to see.

do: Read the poem out loud once.
Read Think About It.
Keep your answer in mind as you read.
how.why: The speaker of a poem and the narrator of a book are both voices a writer creates.

do: Tap a word.
Then tap the root it belongs to.
Match all four words.
how.why: Finding the root tells you what a long word is about.

do: Read each sentence from the book.
Look for clues around the word.
Tap a word, then tap its meaning.
how.why: Clues in the sentence can tell you what a word means.

do: Tap the first word of each appositive.
Open Check under Precise nouns.
Answer Show What You Know in the box.
how.why: Appositives and precise nouns both tell the reader exactly who or what.

do: Say each word and stop after the first beat.
Tap a word, then tap its column.
how.why: Open and closed syllables help you read and spell long words.

do: Read Chapters 3 and 4 first.
Answer each question in 2 or more sentences.
Use details from the chapters as evidence.
how.why: These questions check the events and what Isaac's voice tells you about them.

do: Pick one moment from your Day 1 list.
Write 3 to 5 sentences with I.
Put one thought or feeling inside.
how.why: Writing from the inside is how Isaac pulls you into his story.
how.use: Next lesson you will revise this draft.

do: Read what courage means.
Read how courage shows up in this week's chapters.
Watch for courage while you read. Nothing to write here.
Tap Listen, or read the chapter introduction.
Open your book and read Chapters 3–4.
Answer the Quick Check.
Do the RWM box: read the sentence, then answer as a reader and as a writer.

glossary.meaning: details from the book that show something is true

miss.cedar: Say ce-dar. The first beat, ce, ends on the vowel e, and the e says its name. That makes it open.
miss.willow: Say wil-low. The first beat, wil, ends on the consonant l, and the i is short. That makes it closed.
miss.bible: Say Bi-ble. The first beat, Bi, ends on the vowel i, and the i says its name. That makes it open.
miss.stickball: Say stick-ball. The first beat, stick, ends on the consonant sound k, and the i is short. That makes it closed.
miss.cypress: Say cy-press. The first beat, cy, ends on y. Here y works as a vowel and says a long i. That makes it open.
miss.chicken: Say chick-en. The first beat, chick, ends on the consonant sound k, and the i is short. That makes it closed.
miss.comet: Say com-et. The first beat, com, ends on the consonant m, and the o is short. That makes it closed.
miss.hollow: Say hol-low. The first beat, hol, ends on the consonant l, and the o is short. That makes it closed.

game.title: Stones in the River
game.look: Each stone holds a word. Syllable stones: split the word after its first beat, then say open or closed. Root stones: tap only the letters of the root hiding inside the word. Every word you finish lights a stone, and your crossing keeps going all week.
game.doneLine: Every stone for today is lit.
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 stones today

do: Say the word slowly.
Tap the gap where the first beat ends.
Tap Open or Closed.
Tap Next stone.
how.why: New words, same rule. If you can split a word you never practiced, you know the rule.

art.title: Bayou Teche, Louisiana
art.alt: A painting of a quiet river in evening light, with tall trees and hanging moss along the banks reflected in still water.
art.look: Joseph Rusling Meeker painted this river in Louisiana in 1883, about fifty years after Isaac's story. Louisiana is next door to Mississippi, and its rivers and trees look much like the ones in the Choctaw Nation. Look at the still water and the light. In Chapter 3, Isaac's mother tells him the river and the land are their home, not the house.
art.creator: Joseph Rusling Meeker
art.lookBtn: Tap to learn about this painting

checks.q: Which of these really happens in Chapter 4, and is not one of Isaac's visions?

options.t: Mister Jonah's hair bursts into flames.
options.why: That was a vision in Chapter 2. It came after the warm shiver, and when Isaac looked again, Mister Jonah had no burns. In Chapter 4 Isaac tells you the difference: “I felt no shiver. This was real.”

options.t: Old Woman falls into the river and stops moving.
options.why: That was a vision in Chapter 3. When Isaac opened his eyes again, she was laughing and playing in the river. In Chapter 4 Isaac tells you the difference: “I felt no shiver. This was real.”

options.t: Isaac's hair catches fire and he smothers it with his blanket.
options.why: Isaac tells you, “I felt no shiver. This was real.” The visions always come after the warm shiver.
